Here's my take on OpenAI dots vs. the other personal agents:

1. These are really two separate races. dots and Grok Bot are going after work tasks. Muse is going after personal tasks. So I don't think dots competes directly with Muse.

2. Dots' biggest advantage is that it lives inside ChatGPT. My onboarding was seamless because everything was already connected. And with my ChatGPT memory and Astra behind it, it answers big questions like "What should I do to grow my business?" better than other agents.

3. I also think of dots as ChatGPT's official chief of staff agent. My favorite way to use it is to call it on a walk, ask "What should I take care of today?", then have it hand work off to my other ChatGPT threads.

4. In contrast, chatting with my dot in the app is a worse experience. Since it's juggling several tasks at once, it's hard to tell which one it's responding to. I prefer Grok Bot (where each bot works on one thing at a time) or talking to my dot in Slack (which has more obvious conversation threading).

5. I'm a broken record about this, but cramming Codex, Work, dots, Spaces, Pages, and more all into ChatGPT is overwhelming. My hunch is everyone at OpenAI is agent-pilled, so it's hard to take a step back and think about how casual users will learn all this stuff. This is the biggest gap imo - OpenAI needs to think a lot harder about onboarding for normal users. My mom will have no idea how to use any of this.

📌 I talk more about all this in my full dots review and tutorial here: https://t.co/kUtg3RPk7l

I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today.

Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed.

At the command center, people sit in front of six screens with a paper flight chart above them, trying to make the calls on weather and routing.

His example: four planes reach the same runway at the same time and only one can land. See it two hours out, speed up two, slow one down, and each one lands when the runway is open. "Like, not complicated stuff, but we don't do any of this."

Paper and pencil and minimal human augmentation from software looks like this: Say an airport can take 15 planes in a 15 minute window. "Well, the airlines will schedule 32." He says he's handing the airlines that data and asking them to spread out.

The tool is SMART, from Air Space Intelligence, a small company he says competed with the biggest companies and won. It predicts. His stage example: a 2.5 hour ground stop might only need 45 minutes. He's taken heat for supposedly handing air traffic control to AI. Duffy's answer? "it's dumb AI, not smart AI." Controllers still make every call.

None of this needs a breakthrough. It needs the will of the people to know they need to use software and be ok with AI augmentation instead of insisting on a paper chart and copper wire.

tweets.text:
There's a huge opportunity right now in being the deployment layer for AI into the economy. The amount of work it takes to change out workflows in enterprises tends to be far greater than anyone realizes or would prefer. Clearly this is what the applied layer of AI is going to look like in the form of software and agents, but also it opens up new services firms opportunities.

Legacy systems need to be moved to the cloud, data organization and access needs to be updated, software needs to be connected to agents in new ways, workflows need to be reengineered for agents, HITL needs to be figured out for the process, evals need to be generated and maintained, and the entire system needs to be continually updated as new models get released and new capabilities emerge. And the full list may even be longer.

AI is not the same as just deploying software. Software you generally did the implementation of an existing, well understood category of technology, then stepped back and the customer kept running. With AI agents, you're delivering actual work augmentation to the organization, which has a completely different set of complexities associated with it. You're no longer deploying tools that the company is merely enabled by, you're deploying work output in a process. Completely different implementation and enablement process.

As a result, this is going to open up lots of new kinds of firms and plays for existing firms to diffuse AI into organizations. We're going to see approaches by industry, by size of company, and by problem inside of companies. Traditional SIs will modernize and adapt (some will clearly not adapt as well), and new entrants will also be founded in this period that take advantage of this window. Great time to be an FDE or FDE firm.

Two random honest thoughts on the market right now..

First is on people: It's harder than ever to find missionaries. I'm seeing people leave the companies they have cofounded to join the "obvious" winners. Public CEOs are leaving for positions at labs. Founders leaving and rejoining neolabs at a moment's notice. Companies getting Windsurf-ed where only the choice people are getting to join the future company. Founders raising tranched valuations without worrying about the next employee that will join them will have 409As that make early exercising impossible. 

As early stage VCs, we are often just betting on people. And, when those people leave on a dime's notice, then the remaining company (usually) becomes a shell. It seems like a great time to be a mercenary, and everyone feels like one even though there are missionaries out there. 

Second is on defensibility: There's a lot of chatter on moats, so I won't re-litigate the matter here. But the thing that I want to call out is given the pace of what's happening the moat is no longer "one" thing. Like if you really think about it especially in the app layer - the harness is like a thousand small things done well. And, a lot of it is invisible. And given the competition is so fierce and new entrants overnight, you really have to dig into the details to figure out why a given company is different. What is their edge, and their combined edge across product, tech and GTM. 

And often times even with that, you end up going back to "well the real defensibility is the founders". And in those founders the defensibility is their speed of execution and being able to adapt to the market. That has become the new bar for every founder out there, given there are no "blue ocean" markets. And even if there are, any company with a LITTLE bit of heat, will have a lot of competitiors overnight. 

Even though I think I have a pretty good sense on finding the best people who have founder market fit, I find this current climate really hard and it's testing all my priors (and patience) at the same time. 

I know it's not true, but feels like everyone is in it to grab the bag and not really care about their legacy of what they want to build (please reach out if you do).

This new technical deep dive from the Near One team breaks down SPICE, Separation of Consensus and Execution.

SPICE is a significant architectural upgrade for NEAR Protocol that decouples transaction ordering, data availability, and execution. Execution moves off the critical path of block production, so the chain can produce blocks at a high rate while execution and data availability run asynchronously.

When SPICE launches, NEAR will have faster blocks, lower latency across near.​com and NEAR Intents, and support for longer-running, more complex transactions. It also lays the groundwork for atomic execution across shards.

tweets.text: metamask disclosed an infrastructure incident on september 30 and is pulling its affected ethereum validators, the machines that stake eth and earn rewards for lido. lido expects the eth back, but exiting, withdrawing and restaking could take about 45 days. stETH spreads rewards and penalties across lido's whole pool, so every holder shares the gap. if the full 230,528 eth footprint, 2.34% of the pool, earned nothing for 45 days, that's about 642 eth in lost rewards. how much stake was actually affected is unconfirmed, and any penalties would add to the cost.

ducat, a new token on robinhood chain, sells discounted bonds to fund its treasury. its rules only require stablecoin reserves to cover a redemption reference, now $1, times total supply after each sale. bonds can therefore be issued below existing backing per token, so the treasury and supply can both grow while backing per token falls. redemptions pay 99% of the lower of that reference or stablecoin reserves per token, so weaker backing can cut the payout even though the reference only moves up.

u.s. tax rules treat crypto as property, so spending it, even on network fees, can trigger a taxable gain or loss. a circulating draft from senator steve daines would waive that for qualifying dollar-stablecoin purchases of goods and services, and for network fees of $10 or less per transaction. traders bear the tradeoff. a loss couldn't be deducted right away if they buy the same asset within 30 days before or after selling. final language is unconfirmed.

坏消息：Dev 自己发了蹭特朗普的AI概念币，自己内幕交易了。 
好消息：Dev 自己卖飞了。

10 天前当懂王提议给 AI 改名时，我们提到大概率会有人光速发同名 Meme 来接住这波叙事。

这不，Solana 上的 $SI (Super Inu) 顺势起飞，一路狂飙，市值最高冲到了 6000 万美元。

但是，据 @bubblemaps  刚刚扒出的链上真相，这个 Dev 拿到了黑色幽默的剧本：

蹭上顶级叙事的 $SI 开发者，一开始就没安好心。他用 8 个其他钱包开盘偷偷狙击了 32% 的天量筹码，准备割一把就跑。

他确实跑了，但筹码砸早了，当时仅仅套现了 2.4 万美元。

而如果他拿到了今天，这笔筹码价值 1500 万美元。

更有意思的是，卖飞之后,这位 Dev 很难受，甚至还试图高价买回来，但一切都太晚了。

小编想起之前牛来的 Dev 也没赚到钱。

所以很多时候， Dev 亲手发出的王炸，却用几万块钱的格局把它当对三打了出去；在大机会本来就不多的 meme 市场里，赚少了也是一种亏钱🤡

AI 项目还没来得及换马甲，域名圈的炒家已经先把盘子给拉飞了。

特朗普把 AI 改叫 SI 后，意外承接这波流量的，是远在欧洲的小国斯洛文尼亚。因为 .si 正好是斯洛文尼亚的国家顶级域名。

据当地域名管理机构统计，在特朗普宣布改名之前，.si 的注册量大约每月 3,500 个；宣布改名后，注册量飙升到日均 3,700 个。截至 9 月 29 日，.si 域名总量已经突破 22 万个。

这跟当年安圭拉靠 .ai 躺赚、黑山的 .me 被全球网友玩出花如出一辙。

ENA 的“新晋喊单王”换人了。

刚刚渣打银行发研报，直接把 ENA 的目标价喊到了2028年将达到 2 美元，和现价比还有10倍差距。

比起 Arthur Hayes 之前喊的 0.5 刀，传统金融开喊显然画的饼更大。

从研报公开的部分来看，渣打喊2刀的理由看着还是非常传统和宏观。

比如其预测链上 RWA 规模将从目前的 400 亿美元，在 2028 年底狂飙至 2 万亿美元。

而目前生息稳定币仅占稳定币总市值的 5%， USDe 作为史上最快达成百亿市值的稳定币，将吃下最大的增量份额。

加之 Ethena 近期推出的回购计划，将把协议净收入用于回购并销毁 ethereum:0x57e114b691db790c35207b2e685d4a43181e6061 ，所以更加看涨。

不过，这个喊单逻辑在短期可能还是有问题。

第一，触发回购的硬性门槛，是 USDe 供应量必须达到 75 亿美元，而目前的规模仅在 49 亿徘徊。
在那之前，协议收益仍主要分给 sUSDe 质押者和渠道，不会变成 ENA 买盘。就算过线，第一档也只是从总收益里抽 5% 做回购，不是一开闸就全额回购。

第二， ENA 在10 月 5 日将有高达 14 亿枚（约占流通盘 14%）的 VC 和投资者筹码一次性集中解锁，谨防 dump。

tweets.text: Inspired by @HesterPeirce’s recent speech: https://t.co/jShXWcAZPy

One of the biggest killers of innovation is being blinded by hypothetical downsides. It’s easy to raise concerns about why something might be risky. It's much harder to consider the potential harm of putting too many restrictions in place.

Consider the de facto ban on nuclear with the establishment of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Today we'd have a modern, robust electric grid, and much higher economic growth, if we had kept building nuclear power plants.

All around us we see systems that were well-intentioned when they were introduced, but had unintended consequences.

How things fail:
- Asymmetric error costs - approve a bad reactor or drug and you’re famous. Yet if you block a good one, no one ever knows.

- Process as a veto - hourly fees, multi-step license applications, EPA reviews. Endless delays erode capital.

- Worst-case models treated as fact - LNT radiation, any sonic boom is unacceptable, etc.

- Rules written for the last accident, applied to the next design - we see this in everything from nuclear to financial services.

Change is uncomfortable, but if we stop progress, we do a disservice to our ancestors who tolerated discomfort to bring us the modern age. We owe it to them to continue making progress.
